overview: Alerting design is the discipline of deciding which conditions in a data platform should interrupt a human, how urgently, and what that human is expected to do about it, so that every notification is worth acting on.

For data engineering on-call, good alerting distinguishes between what breaks the promise made to consumers (freshness, correctness, volume) and what merely happened internally (a retried task, a transient CPU spike), and only pages when a human is genuinely needed.

Alert fatigue is the failure mode where an on-call is flooded with low-value, non-actionable, or duplicate pages until they start ignoring alerts, which means the one page that matters gets missed; fighting it is a first-class reliability concern, not a cosmetic one.
learningObjectives: Distinguish symptom-based (user-facing) alerting from cause-based alerting and explain why symptom-based paging reduces noise.
Design SLO- and error-budget-driven alerts, including multi-window multi-burn-rate rules, and understand the trade-offs of each window pair.
Apply severity tiers, routing, deduplication, grouping, silencing, and inhibition in tools like Alertmanager and PagerDuty to keep pages actionable.
Measure alert fatigue with concrete metrics (pages per shift, actionable percentage, MTTA) and run a systematic noise-reduction loop.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Alerting design is the systematic specification of monitoring signals, thresholds, severity, routing, and suppression logic that converts observed system and data state into human-directed notifications, optimized so that every page is urgent, actionable, and unique. Alert fatigue is the measurable degradation of on-call responsiveness caused by exposure to excessive, non-actionable, or redundant alerts, mitigated by symptom-based and SLO-driven alerting, deduplication, grouping, inhibition, and continuous tuning against fatigue metrics.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of alerting like the warning lights in a car. A good car only lights up the dashboard when you actually need to do something now, like 'engine overheating', and it does not beep every time a sensor twitches. A bad car would flash forty lights for tiny things until you tape over the dashboard and then miss the real fire. Alerting design is about wiring your data pipelines so the only things that wake someone up at 3 AM are things that a human must fix right now, and everything else becomes a quiet ticket or a log entry.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Threshold-based alerting on host metrics (CPU, disk, memory) dominated the Nagios era of the 2000s and produced enormous noise because it alerted on causes rather than user impact. Google's Site Reliability Engineering book (2016) popularized symptom-based alerting and SLO/error-budget-driven paging, and the follow-up SRE Workbook (2018) formalized multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts. The Prometheus and Alertmanager ecosystem (~2015 onward) brought label-based routing, grouping, and inhibition to open source, while PagerDuty and Opsgenie industrialized escalation and on-call scheduling. In data engineering the same ideas arrived later through data observability tools (Monte Carlo, ~2019) and pipeline-native tests (dbt tests, Great Expectations), reframing freshness and volume as the data equivalent of user-facing symptoms.

whyItMatters.business: Missed critical alerts cause data downtime that corrupts executive dashboards, delays regulatory filings, and breaks customer-facing data products; disciplined alerting protects revenue and trust by ensuring the right incident is caught fast while noise does not bury it.
whyItMatters.engineering: Actionable, symptom-based alerts turn ambiguous 3 AM pages into a clear next step tied to a runbook, cutting mean time to acknowledge and resolve and reducing the cognitive load that causes on-call burnout and attrition.
whyItMatters.scalability: As the number of pipelines, tables, and sources grows into the thousands, per-object cause-based alerts explode into thousands of pages; SLO-driven and grouped alerting keeps the page volume roughly constant with the number of user-facing promises, not the number of components.
whyItMatters.cost: Every unnecessary page has a real cost in engineer time, context-switching, and eventual turnover; reducing non-actionable alerts directly lowers operational spend, and catching a burn early via burn-rate alerts avoids expensive full error-budget exhaustion and backfills.
whyItMatters.reliability: Alerting is the sensory system of reliability: SLOs make the target explicit, error budgets make the tolerance explicit, and burn-rate alerts make degradation detectable early, so reliability becomes something you steer rather than something you discover after the fact.

coreComponents.name: Alert Rule
coreComponents.definition: A declarative condition evaluated against metrics or data-quality signals that, when true for a defined duration, produces a firing alert with labels and annotations.
coreComponents.purpose: To convert continuous observed state into a discrete, labeled signal that downstream routing and suppression can act on.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Define the expression (for example a burn-rate threshold), the `for` duration to avoid flapping, severity labels, and annotations carrying the runbook link and summary.
coreComponents.examples: A Prometheus rule that fires when the 1-hour and 5-minute error-budget burn rate both exceed 14.4x for a 99.9% SLO; a freshness rule that fires when `time() - pipeline_last_success_timestamp > 3600`.

coreComponents.name: Severity Tier
coreComponents.definition: A classification (typically P1 through P4, or critical/warning/info) that encodes urgency and the required response channel.
coreComponents.purpose: To decide whether a signal should page a human immediately, open a ticket for business hours, or simply be logged.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Map each condition to page-vs-ticket-vs-log, drive routing to the correct escalation policy, and set acknowledgement and resolution expectations.
coreComponents.examples: P1: customer-facing revenue table stale past SLA -> page immediately; P3: a single non-critical dbt model test failed -> ticket; P4: a task retried once and succeeded -> log only.

coreComponents.name: Router and Grouping Engine
coreComponents.definition: The component (Alertmanager or PagerDuty event rules) that receives alerts and decides recipients, groups related alerts, deduplicates, and throttles repeats.
coreComponents.purpose: To ensure alerts reach the owning team and that an alert storm collapses into a single coherent notification.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Match labels to receivers, group by keys such as cluster or pipeline, apply `group_wait`/`group_interval`/`repeat_interval`, and deduplicate by dedup key.
coreComponents.examples: Alertmanager routing `team=ingestion` alerts to a PagerDuty receiver and grouping by `alertname` and `pipeline`; PagerDuty deduplicating repeated events sharing a `dedup_key`.

coreComponents.name: Suppression Logic (Silencing and Inhibition)
coreComponents.definition: Mechanisms that stop lower-value alerts from firing when they are known noise (silence) or are a downstream consequence of a known upstream failure (inhibition).
coreComponents.purpose: To prevent alert storms where one root cause triggers dozens of dependent alerts.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Silence alerts during planned maintenance, and inhibit downstream alerts (for example dbt model failures) when the upstream source (for example Kafka ingestion) is already alerting.
coreComponents.examples: An Alertmanager inhibition rule where a firing `severity=critical` source-outage alert suppresses all `severity=warning` alerts sharing the same `pipeline` label.

coreComponents.name: Escalation Policy and Runbook
coreComponents.definition: The on-call schedule, escalation chain, and the linked documentation describing how to diagnose and remediate a specific alert.
coreComponents.purpose: To guarantee an alert reaches a responder and that the responder knows what to do without reverse-engineering the system at 3 AM.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Rotate on-call, escalate if unacknowledged within a timeout, and attach a concrete, tested runbook to every paging alert.
coreComponents.examples: PagerDuty escalates to the secondary on-call after 10 minutes of no acknowledgement; the alert annotation links to a runbook with exact queries and remediation steps.

internalWorking: A collector (Prometheus, a data-observability agent, or an orchestrator callback) continuously produces time series and signals such as `pipeline_freshness_seconds`, `dbt_test_failures_total`, or SLI success ratios.

The alerting engine evaluates rule expressions on a fixed interval; an expression that is true is held in a pending state for the `for` duration, and only if it remains true does it transition to firing, which filters out momentary spikes.
A firing alert carries labels (team, severity, pipeline, service) and annotations (summary, runbook_url); these labels are the routing key that determines everything downstream.
The router matches labels against a routing tree to select a receiver, then groups alerts sharing configured group-by labels so many related firings collapse into one notification after `group_wait`.

Deduplication uses a dedup key so repeated identical events update the existing incident instead of opening new ones; inhibition rules suppress dependent alerts when a designated source alert is already firing.

The notifier sends the grouped, deduplicated alert to PagerDuty or Opsgenie, which applies the escalation policy, tracks acknowledgement (MTTA), and escalates to the next responder if unacknowledged within the timeout.

Resolution flows back: when the underlying condition clears, a resolve event closes the incident, and the whole lifecycle (fired, acknowledged, resolved) is recorded to compute fatigue and reliability metrics.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: SLIs & pipeline signals (Prometheus / observability / orchestrator callbacks) -> Alert rules evaluate (expression + for) -> Firing alert with labels & annotations -> Router matches receiver -> Group + deduplicate + inhibit -> Notify PagerDuty/Opsgenie -> Escalation policy pages on-call -> Acknowledge (MTTA) -> Runbook remediation -> Resolve event -> Post-incident tuning of thresholds & fatigue metrics
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. An upstream Kafka source stops producing, so the ingestion pipeline's `pipeline_last_success_timestamp` stops advancing and its SLI success ratio drops.

2. A multi-burn-rate SLO rule sees the fast (5m) and slow (1h) burn rates both exceed the fast threshold and, after a short `for`, transitions to firing with `severity=critical, team=ingestion, pipeline=events`.
3. Simultaneously, dozens of downstream dbt models that depend on the events table begin failing freshness tests and would each fire a warning alert.

4. Alertmanager routes the critical ingestion alert to the ingestion team's PagerDuty receiver and, via an inhibition rule, suppresses all the downstream `severity=warning` alerts that share `pipeline=events`, so only one page is sent.

5. PagerDuty deduplicates repeated evaluations under one dedup key, pages the on-call, tracks acknowledgement, and links the runbook; when Kafka recovers and the SLI restores, a resolve event closes the incident and the timeline feeds the fatigue dashboard.

keyTerminology.meaning: Alerting on user-visible impact (data is stale, wrong, or missing) rather than on internal causes (a specific host is at high CPU).
keyTerminology.importance: It is the single biggest lever for noise reduction because it collapses many possible causes into a few meaningful, actionable signals.

keyTerminology.meaning: The allowed amount of unreliability implied by an SLO, computed as 1 minus the SLO target over a window (a 99.9% SLO permits 0.1% failure).
keyTerminology.importance: It turns reliability into a quantity you can spend, and burn-rate alerts fire based on how fast you are consuming it.

keyTerminology.meaning: How fast the error budget is being consumed relative to the rate that would exhaust it exactly at the end of the window; a burn rate of 1 exhausts it precisely on time.
keyTerminology.importance: Alerting on burn rate detects severe degradation early while ignoring slow, tolerable error rates, giving both fast detection and low noise.

keyTerminology.meaning: An alerting pattern that combines a long and a short window at each burn-rate threshold so an alert requires both sustained and recent breach.
keyTerminology.importance: It gives fast detection for severe outages, good precision (few false positives), and fast reset once the issue clears.

keyTerminology.meaning: The average time between an alert paging and a human acknowledging it.
keyTerminology.importance: Rising MTTA is an early signal of alert fatigue: responders are slow because they no longer trust the pages.

keyTerminology.meaning: A stable identifier attached to an alert event so repeated occurrences of the same condition map to one incident.
keyTerminology.importance: It prevents a flapping or repeatedly evaluated condition from opening hundreds of incidents.

keyTerminology.meaning: Suppressing a set of alerts while a designated higher-priority source alert is firing, expressing a known cause-effect relationship.
keyTerminology.importance: It is how a single upstream failure avoids generating an alert storm of dependent downstream alerts.

keyTerminology.meaning: An alert that requires and enables a specific human action; if the responder can do nothing or ignores it safely, it is not actionable.
keyTerminology.importance: Actionability is the acceptance test for whether something should page at all versus become a ticket or a log.

importantConcepts.explanation: What: every candidate alert must be classified into interrupt-now (page), handle-in-business-hours (ticket), or record-only (log). Why: paging is expensive and disruptive, so it must be reserved for urgent, actionable conditions. How: ask 'must a human act within minutes to avoid user-facing harm?' If yes, page; if it can wait, ticket; if no action is needed, log. Pitfall: teams default everything to page, which manufactures fatigue and trains responders to ignore alerts.

What: alert on the effect users experience (stale or wrong data) rather than every internal cause. Why: there are many causes but few symptoms, so symptom alerts are fewer and inherently actionable. How: define alerts on SLIs like freshness, completeness, and success ratio at the consumer boundary. Pitfall: alerting on causes (disk 80% full, one worker restarted) generates volume and often fires for conditions the system tolerates automatically.

importantConcepts.concept: Every page must be actionable and have a runbook
importantConcepts.explanation: What: a paging alert should demand a specific action and link to tested remediation steps. Why: a page with no action is pure noise, and a page with no runbook forces re-diagnosis under stress. How: gate new paging alerts on a written runbook and a clear 'what to do' during review. Pitfall: FYI pages and page-with-no-owner alerts erode trust in the whole system.

importantConcepts.concept: Alert fatigue is measurable and must be steered
importantConcepts.explanation: What: fatigue is not a vibe; it is quantifiable via pages per shift, actionable percentage, and MTTA. Why: what you do not measure you cannot reduce. How: instrument alert lifecycle events, review them in on-call retros, and delete or downgrade the noisiest alerts each cycle. Pitfall: treating a noisy on-call as normal until an engineer quits or a real incident is missed.

variationsAndTypes: **Threshold alerts:** fire when a metric crosses a static bound (for example freshness lag over 1 hour); simple but prone to false positives if the baseline shifts.
**SLO/error-budget alerts:** fire based on how much of the error budget is consumed, tying alerting directly to the reliability promise rather than raw metrics.
**Multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts:** combine a fast and slow window at each burn threshold for high precision and fast detection and reset, the SRE-recommended default for SLOs.
**Anomaly / baseline alerts:** fire when a signal deviates from its learned normal (used by data-observability tools for volume and distribution) to catch unknown-unknowns.
**Freshness/timeliness alerts:** fire when a table or pipeline has not updated within its expected cadence, the data-engineering equivalent of a user-facing symptom.
**Volume/row-count alerts:** fire on unexpected drops or spikes in rows loaded, catching partial loads and duplicate loads.
**Quality alerts:** fire when dbt tests or Great Expectations suites breach thresholds (null spikes, failed uniqueness), gating publication of bad data.
**Heartbeat / dead-man's-switch alerts:** fire when an expected regular signal stops arriving, catching the case where the alerting pipeline itself has died.
advantages: **High signal-to-noise ratio:** symptom-based and SLO-driven alerts page only for conditions that matter to consumers, so responders trust every page.
**Early detection with low false positives:** multi-burn-rate rules catch severe degradation in minutes while ignoring tolerable error rates.
**Storm collapse:** grouping, deduplication, and inhibition turn a cascade of dependent failures into a single coherent page.
**Faster response:** actionable alerts with runbooks reduce MTTA and mean time to resolve because the next step is unambiguous.
**Sustainable on-call:** fewer, higher-value pages reduce burnout and attrition and keep the team responsive when a real incident arrives.
disadvantages: **Design and tuning effort:** SLOs, burn-rate windows, routing trees, and inhibition rules take real engineering time to get right and to maintain.
**Requires good SLIs:** SLO alerting is only as good as the underlying indicators; poorly chosen SLIs page for the wrong things.
**Suppression risk:** aggressive inhibition or silencing can hide a genuinely independent second failure.
**Delayed detection for slow burns:** by design, low burn rates alert as tickets rather than pages, which is correct but can surprise teams expecting instant pages for any error.
**Tooling complexity:** correctly configuring Alertmanager routing, PagerDuty event rules, and dedup keys has a learning curve and is easy to misconfigure.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use SLO- and symptom-based alerting with multi-burn-rate rules for user-facing and business-critical data products where you have meaningful SLIs and a defined reliability target; use grouping, dedup, and inhibition anywhere upstream failures cascade into many downstream objects.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid heavyweight SLO machinery for low-stakes internal or exploratory pipelines where a simple freshness ticket suffices, and avoid aggressive inhibition where downstream failures could be genuinely independent and must be seen separately.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Alerting design is like a hospital's triage and monitoring system. Vital-sign monitors are symptom-based: they alarm when the patient is actually in danger (oxygen dropping), not every time a wire wiggles. Triage assigns severity so a heart attack (P1) interrupts everyone while a sprained wrist (P3) waits in the queue. When one machine's power fails and sets off ten dependent alarms, staff know to fix the power (inhibition) rather than chase ten symptoms. And every alarm has a protocol posted on the wall (a runbook). A ward where every monitor beeps constantly is exactly alert fatigue: nurses tune it out, and the one real emergency gets missed.

commonMisconceptions.reality: Beyond a point, more alerts mean worse monitoring, because non-actionable and duplicate pages train responders to ignore the system, so the real incident is missed. Coverage comes from good SLIs, not alert count.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should page immediately on any error.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A single error, or even a low sustained error rate, is usually within the error budget and should not page. Multi-burn-rate alerting pages fast only for severe budget consumption and routes slow burns to tickets.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Alert fatigue is just people being lazy about on-call.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Fatigue is a predictable, measurable systems problem caused by noisy alert design; it is fixed by symptom-based alerting, suppression, and tuning, not by asking responders to try harder.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Scale alert volume with the number of user-facing promises, not the number of components: define SLO alerts at consumer boundaries, group by pipeline or team, and rely on inhibition so a source outage produces one page regardless of how many downstream tables depend on it.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Make the alerting path itself reliable with heartbeat/dead-man's-switch alerts so a silent Prometheus or Alertmanager outage is detected, and version alert rules alongside pipeline code so changes are reviewed and reversible.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Run Alertmanager in a clustered, gossiping configuration so a single node failure does not drop or duplicate notifications, and ensure resolve events are sent so incidents auto-close even if a scrape is briefly missed.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Monitor the meta-metrics of alerting itself: pages per on-call shift, actionable percentage, MTTA, MTTR, and the top-10 noisiest alerts, and review them every on-call handoff.
productionConsiderations.security: Restrict who can silence or delete alerts and who can edit escalation policies, avoid embedding secrets or raw sensitive data in alert annotations sent to third-party paging tools, and audit silences so alerts are not quietly disabled.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Reduce paging-tool and engineer-time cost by downgrading non-urgent alerts to tickets, deduplicating storms, and deleting always-firing or never-actioned rules; each removed noisy alert lowers both spend and fatigue.
productionConsiderations.performance: Keep rule-evaluation intervals and `for` durations tuned so detection is fast without over-alerting on transients, use recording rules to precompute expensive SLI ratios, and keep routing trees shallow so matching stays fast at scale.

codeExamples.title: Multi-Window Multi-Burn-Rate SLO Alert (Prometheus)
codeExamples.overview: Prometheus alerting rules for a 99.9% availability SLO on a data ingestion service, using the recommended fast and slow burn-rate pairs so severe outages page quickly while slow burns open tickets.
codeExamples.code:
groups:
  - name: ingestion_slo_burn
    rules:
      # Recording rules precompute the error ratio over each window
      - record: job:ingestion_error_ratio:5m
        expr: sum(rate(ingestion_requests_total{status="error"}[5m]))
             / sum(rate(ingestion_requests_total[5m]))
      - record: job:ingestion_error_ratio:1h
        expr: sum(rate(ingestion_requests_total{status="error"}[1h]))
             / sum(rate(ingestion_requests_total[1h]))
      - record: job:ingestion_error_ratio:6h
        expr: sum(rate(ingestion_requests_total{status="error"}[6h]))
             / sum(rate(ingestion_requests_total[6h]))

      # FAST burn: 14.4x over 1h AND 5m -> pages (budget gone in ~2 days)
      - alert: IngestionErrorBudgetBurnFast
        expr: |
          job:ingestion_error_ratio:1h > (14.4 * 0.001)
          and
          job:ingestion_error_ratio:5m > (14.4 * 0.001)
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: critical
          team: ingestion
          pipeline: events
        annotations:
          summary: "Fast error-budget burn on ingestion (14.4x)"
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.internal/ingestion/error-budget-burn"

      # SLOW burn: 6x over 6h AND 1h -> ticket (creeping degradation)
      - alert: IngestionErrorBudgetBurnSlow
        expr: |
          job:ingestion_error_ratio:6h > (6 * 0.001)
          and
          job:ingestion_error_ratio:1h > (6 * 0.001)
        for: 15m
        labels:
          severity: warning
          team: ingestion
          pipeline: events
        annotations:
          summary: "Slow error-budget burn on ingestion (6x)"
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.internal/ingestion/error-budget-burn"
codeExamples.breakdown: The SLO target is 99.9%, so the error-budget fraction is 0.001. A burn rate of 14.4 means the budget for a 30-day window is consumed in about 2 days, so it merits a page; 6x means about 5 days and merits a ticket. Each alert requires BOTH a long-window and a short-window breach: the long window gives precision (the problem is sustained) and the short window gives fast reset (once fixed, the 5m ratio drops quickly and the alert clears). Recording rules precompute the ratios so the alert expressions stay cheap. Labels drive routing and severity; the runbook_url annotation makes the page actionable.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: During a real outage, IngestionErrorBudgetBurnFast transitions pending -> firing after 2 minutes and Alertmanager sends one critical page. A brief blip that clears within 2 minutes never fires. A slow 0.7% sustained error rate opens IngestionErrorBudgetBurnSlow as a warning/ticket instead of paging.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting to require both windows, which reintroduces false positives; hardcoding the SLO fraction in many places instead of a single source; setting `for` too long so detection lags; not adding recording rules, which makes evaluation expensive at scale.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Parameterize the SLO target and burn multipliers via a generator/template so many services share one definition; add a second fast pair (for example 6x over 30m and 5m) for slightly-less-severe fast burns; use recording rules for every window and alert only on the recorded series.

codeExamples.title: Alertmanager Routing, Grouping, and Inhibition
codeExamples.overview: An Alertmanager configuration that routes by team, groups related alerts, throttles repeats, and inhibits downstream data-quality warnings when the upstream source is already alerting critical.
codeExamples.code:
route:
  receiver: default-ticket
  group_by: ['alertname', 'pipeline']
  group_wait: 30s        # wait to batch related alerts before first notify
  group_interval: 5m     # min time between notifications for a group
  repeat_interval: 4h    # re-page an unresolved incident every 4h
  routes:
    - matchers:
        - severity = "critical"
      receiver: pagerduty-oncall
      group_by: ['pipeline']
      continue: false
    - matchers:
        - severity = "warning"
        - team = "ingestion"
      receiver: jira-ticket

receivers:
  - name: default-ticket
    webhook_configs:
      - url: "https://hooks.internal/ticket"
  - name: pagerduty-oncall
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key: "<PD_INTEGRATION_KEY>"
        severity: critical
        dedup_key: '{{ .CommonLabels.pipeline }}-{{ .CommonLabels.alertname }}'
  - name: jira-ticket
    webhook_configs:
      - url: "https://hooks.internal/jira"

# Suppress downstream dbt/quality warnings when the source is already critical
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers:
      - severity = "critical"
      - alertname = "IngestionErrorBudgetBurnFast"
    target_matchers:
      - severity = "warning"
    equal: ['pipeline']
codeExamples.breakdown: The top-level route sets defaults; child routes override for critical (page via PagerDuty) and for ingestion warnings (open a Jira ticket). group_by collapses alerts sharing alertname and pipeline into one notification; group_wait batches a burst, group_interval throttles updates, and repeat_interval re-pages unresolved incidents so nothing is silently forgotten. The PagerDuty dedup_key built from pipeline+alertname ensures repeated firings map to a single incident. The inhibition rule is the storm-killer: while the critical upstream burn alert fires, every warning sharing the same pipeline label is suppressed, so one Kafka outage does not generate a page per downstream table.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A source outage produces exactly one PagerDuty incident for the pipeline; the dozens of downstream warning alerts are visible in Alertmanager but inhibited (not notified). Ingestion warnings that are NOT inhibited become Jira tickets. Repeated evaluations of the same condition update the one incident rather than opening new ones.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Missing `equal` labels on inhibition, which either inhibits too broadly or not at all; overly broad group_by that merges unrelated incidents; too-short repeat_interval that re-pages aggressively; putting a real routing_key in version control instead of a secret.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep the routing tree shallow and match on a small set of stable labels; use separate receivers per team so ownership is explicit; test routing with `amtool config routes test`; store the PagerDuty routing key in a secret manager and template it in.

codeExamples.title: Airflow on_failure_callback That Pages PagerDuty With a Dedup Key
codeExamples.overview: An Airflow callback that fires an Events API v2 alert to PagerDuty only for tasks tagged critical, using a stable dedup key so retries and repeated failures collapse into one incident.
codeExamples.code:
import requests

PD_EVENTS_URL = "https://events.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue"
PD_ROUTING_KEY = "<PD_ROUTING_KEY>"  # inject via env/secret, not literal

def page_on_failure(context):
    ti = context["task_instance"]
    dag_id = ti.dag_id
    task_id = ti.task_id
    run_id = context["run_id"]

    # Only page for tasks explicitly marked critical
    if not ti.task.params.get("critical", False):
        return

    # Stable dedup key: same failing task+dag collapses into one incident
    dedup_key = f"airflow:{dag_id}:{task_id}"

    payload = {
        "routing_key": PD_ROUTING_KEY,
        "event_action": "trigger",
        "dedup_key": dedup_key,
        "payload": {
            "summary": f"[P1] {dag_id}.{task_id} failed (run {run_id})",
            "severity": "critical",
            "source": "airflow",
            "component": dag_id,
            "group": "data-pipelines",
            "custom_details": {
                "log_url": ti.log_url,
                "try_number": ti.try_number,
                "runbook": f"https://runbooks.internal/{dag_id}",
            },
        },
    }
    resp = requests.post(PD_EVENTS_URL, json=payload, timeout=10)
    resp.raise_for_status()

# Usage in a DAG:
# task = PythonOperator(
#     task_id="load_revenue",
#     python_callable=load_revenue,
#     params={"critical": True},
#     on_failure_callback=page_on_failure,
# )
codeExamples.breakdown: The callback receives Airflow's task context. It first gates on a `critical` param so only business-critical tasks page and everything else stays a log/ticket. The dedup_key is derived from dag_id and task_id (not run_id) so that all retries and repeated daily failures of the same task collapse into a single PagerDuty incident instead of one per attempt. The payload follows PagerDuty Events API v2, embedding the log URL, try number, and a runbook link so the page is immediately actionable. `event_action=trigger` opens/updates the incident; a corresponding resolve call (dedup_key reused with event_action=resolve) in an on_success or SLA callback would auto-close it.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: When a critical task fails and retries three times, PagerDuty shows ONE incident (all retries share the dedup key) with the summary, log URL, and runbook. A non-critical task failing sends nothing. On the next successful run, a resolve event (if wired) closes the incident.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using run_id in the dedup key, which re-opens a new incident per run and creates noise; paging on every task by default; blocking the scheduler on a slow HTTP call without a timeout; hardcoding the routing key.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Send a resolve event on recovery so incidents auto-close and MTTR is accurate; batch by DAG rather than per-task where one DAG failure implies many task failures; route through Alertmanager or an events gateway instead of calling PagerDuty directly so grouping/inhibition still apply.

codeExamples.title: Computing Burn Rate and Fatigue Metrics in Python
codeExamples.overview: Utility functions that compute error-budget burn rate for an SLO and summarize alert-fatigue metrics (pages per shift, actionable percentage, MTTA) from an incident log.
codeExamples.breakdown: burn_rate divides the observed error rate by the error budget (1 - SLO): a 1.44% error rate against a 99.9% SLO yields exactly 14.4x, matching the fast-page threshold. time_to_exhaust converts a burn rate into how many days of a rolling window it would take to consume the whole budget, which is how burn multipliers are chosen (14.4x exhausts a 30-day window in ~2 days). fatigue_report reduces an incident log into the three headline fatigue metrics: pages per shift (volume), actionable percentage (quality), and MTTA (trust/responsiveness). These are the numbers you review at every on-call retro to decide which alerts to delete or downgrade.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Running the script prints `14.4x? 14.4` and `exhaust days 2.1`. Calling fatigue_report on a shift with 12 incidents, 5 actionable, over 3 shifts might return {'pages_per_shift': 4.0, 'actionable_pct': 41.7, 'mtta_seconds': ...}, flagging a noisy rotation.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Dividing by zero when no incidents were acknowledged; mixing timezones in timestamps so MTTA is wrong; counting auto-resolved noise as actionable; treating a low actionable percentage as acceptable.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Feed these metrics into a dashboard and alert (a meta-alert) when actionable_pct drops below a target or pages_per_shift exceeds a threshold; join with the incident's alertname to rank the noisiest rules for deletion.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A fintech data team runs a revenue and fraud pipeline: Kafka feeds raw events, Spark aggregates them, dbt models build the marts, and Snowflake serves customer-facing dashboards under a '99.9% fresh by 6 AM' SLA. The on-call was drowning: over 30 pages per shift, most from cause-based host alerts and cascading dbt failures, so MTTA had crept up and a genuine stale-revenue incident was missed for hours. The goal is to redesign alerting so only actionable, symptom-based conditions page, upstream failures do not spawn storms, and fatigue is measured and driven down.
endToEndExample.inputData: Prometheus metrics for the ingestion and Spark jobs (request/error counts, success timestamps), dbt test results, Great Expectations validation outputs on the marts, and an incident log exported from PagerDuty (triggered/acked/resolved times, actionable flags).
endToEndExample.architecture: SLIs are exported to Prometheus; recording rules compute error ratios and freshness lag. SLO burn-rate and freshness alert rules feed Alertmanager, which routes by team, groups by pipeline, deduplicates, and inhibits downstream warnings when an upstream source is critical. Critical alerts page PagerDuty; warnings open Jira tickets; info is logged. A weekly job computes fatigue metrics from the incident log and publishes them to Grafana.
processingSteps: 1. Define SLOs at the consumer boundary: 99.9% of daily runs fresh by 6 AM and 99.9% success ratio on the ingestion service, and derive error budgets from them.
2. Replace host/cause alerts with symptom alerts: freshness lag on the revenue mart, multi-burn-rate SLO alerts on ingestion, and Great Expectations quality gates on the marts.
3. Classify every alert into page/ticket/log and attach a runbook URL and owning team label to each; only P1/P2 symptoms page.
4. Configure Alertmanager grouping by pipeline and an inhibition rule so a critical Kafka/ingestion burn suppresses the dozens of downstream dbt freshness warnings.
5. Wire the Airflow on_failure_callback to page (with a stable dedup key) only for tasks marked critical, and send resolve events on recovery so incidents auto-close.
6. Instrument the incident log and compute pages-per-shift, actionable percentage, and MTTA weekly, reviewing the top-10 noisiest alerts at each on-call handoff and deleting or downgrading them.
endToEndExample.output: A lean alerting configuration where a single Kafka outage produces one actionable P1 page with a runbook instead of 40 cascading warnings, non-urgent issues become tickets, and a live Grafana dashboard shows fatigue metrics trending down.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Grafana dashboards track SLO compliance and remaining error budget per pipeline, plus the meta-metrics of alerting: pages per shift, actionable percentage, MTTA, MTTR, and a ranked list of the noisiest alertnames. A dead-man's-switch alert confirms the alerting pipeline itself is alive.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Upstream failures inhibit downstream warnings to prevent storms; retries share a dedup key so one incident represents one problem; planned maintenance uses scheduled silences; and if Prometheus or Alertmanager goes silent, the heartbeat alert fires so blind spots are caught.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Pages per shift dropped from over 30 to about 4, actionable percentage rose from roughly 20% to over 80%, and MTTA fell sharply because responders once again trust every page. The next real stale-revenue incident was caught and resolved within minutes via a single, runbook-linked page instead of being lost in noise.

industryUseCases.problem: Traditional cause-based, threshold alerting on machine metrics generated overwhelming noise and paged for conditions users never experienced.
industryUseCases.solution: Google's SRE practice codified symptom-based, SLO- and error-budget-driven alerting, and the SRE Workbook introduced multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts as the recommended pattern.
industryUseCases.benefits: Page volume tracks user-facing reliability rather than component count, giving fast detection of severe outages with high precision and dramatically fewer false pages, which sustains on-call health.

industryUseCases.problem: At massive microservice and data-pipeline scale, per-component alerts and duplicate signals threatened to bury real incidents in noise.
industryUseCases.solution: Netflix invested in automated anomaly detection and alert correlation/deduplication (Atlas metrics platform and related tooling) so related signals collapse and only meaningful, correlated incidents surface.
industryUseCases.benefits: Fewer, higher-signal alerts and faster root-cause identification, allowing a relatively small on-call to operate an enormous streaming and data platform.

industryUseCases.problem: Data teams learned about freshness, volume, and schema incidents only after stakeholders complained, and naive threshold checks produced noisy false alarms.
industryUseCases.solution: A data-observability platform that learns baselines for freshness, volume, and distribution and alerts on anomalies with lineage-aware grouping so one root cause is not reported as many downstream alerts.
industryUseCases.benefits: Symptom-level data incidents are detected automatically with reduced noise and lineage-based deduplication, cutting time-to-detection and easing on-call load for data teams.

industryUseCases.problem: Customers suffered alert storms where a single infrastructure failure triggered floods of duplicate and dependent alerts across tools.
industryUseCases.solution: Event Intelligence features (deduplication by key, alert grouping, and intelligent triage) that collapse related events into single incidents and suppress noise before it reaches responders.
industryUseCases.benefits: Responders receive consolidated, actionable incidents instead of storms, lowering MTTA and reducing burnout across on-call teams.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Anchor alert count to user-facing promises: define SLO and freshness alerts at consumer boundaries rather than per host or per table, use recording rules to precompute SLI ratios cheaply, and rely on grouping and inhibition so a fan-out of downstream dependencies still yields one page. Generate alert rules from templates so thousands of pipelines share a handful of definitions.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Run Alertmanager as a gossiping cluster so no single node loss drops or duplicates notifications, make paging callbacks idempotent via stable dedup keys so retries collapse, and always send resolve events so incidents self-close even if an intermediate scrape is missed.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Deploy redundant Prometheus scrapers and a clustered Alertmanager behind the same routing config, use PagerDuty escalation policies so an unacknowledged page escalates to a secondary responder, and keep on-call schedules and runbooks in durable, replicated stores.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Version alert rules, routing trees, and inhibition config in git so the entire alerting stack can be rebuilt from source; retain incident history so post-incident reviews and fatigue trends survive tooling migrations; and keep a documented failover path if the primary paging provider is down.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Use recording rules for expensive burn-rate and ratio computations, tune evaluation intervals and `for` durations to balance detection speed against transient noise, keep routing trees shallow with matches on a few stable labels, and avoid high-cardinality labels that blow up series and slow evaluation.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Cut both paging-tool spend and engineer time by deleting always-firing or never-actioned rules, downgrading non-urgent pages to tickets, and deduplicating storms; each removed noisy alert reduces cost and fatigue simultaneously. Tier alerting rigor by data-product value.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Store PagerDuty/Opsgenie routing keys in a secret manager and template them into config, restrict who can silence, delete, or edit escalation policies, audit all silences so alerts are not quietly disabled, and avoid embedding secrets or raw sensitive/PII values in alert summaries sent to third-party tools.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Treat alerting as a product with its own SLIs: monitor pages per on-call shift, actionable percentage, MTTA, MTTR, alert precision/recall against real incidents, and the top noisy alerts, and expose remaining error budget per SLO on dashboards.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Map data symptoms to alerts: freshness (table not updated on cadence), volume (row-count drop/spike vs baseline), and quality (dbt tests, Great Expectations null/uniqueness breaches) each become severity-tiered alerts that gate publication, with inhibition so an upstream freshness failure suppresses redundant downstream quality warnings.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log every alert-lifecycle event (fired, grouped, inhibited, acknowledged, resolved) with pipeline and severity context to compute fatigue metrics; ensure every paging alert carries a runbook URL and owning team; and run a heartbeat/dead-man's-switch alert so a silent alerting pipeline is itself detected.

recommendedPractices: **Alert on symptoms, not causes:** page on user-visible impact (stale, wrong, or missing data) rather than every internal metric so alerts are few and actionable.
**Drive paging from SLOs and error budgets:** use multi-window multi-burn-rate rules so severe burns page and slow burns become tickets.
**Classify every alert as page, ticket, or log:** reserve paging for urgent, actionable conditions and demote the rest.
**Attach a runbook and an owner to every paging alert:** a page with no next step and no owner is noise.
**Use grouping, deduplication, and inhibition** so an upstream failure produces one page instead of a downstream storm.
engineeringStandards: Alert rules, routing trees, and inhibition config live in version control and are code-reviewed alongside pipeline changes.
Every critical data product has defined SLIs/SLOs and a named on-call owner with an escalation policy.
New paging alerts are not merged without a written, tested runbook and an actionability justification.
A heartbeat/dead-man's-switch alert protects the alerting pipeline itself against silent failure.
designRecommendations: Prefer the two fast (14.4x) and slow (6x) multi-burn-rate pairs from the SRE Workbook as a sane default, tuned per SLO window.
Group by stable labels such as pipeline or team and keep routing trees shallow for fast, predictable matching.
Express known cause-effect relationships as inhibition rules (upstream critical suppresses downstream warnings).
Tier alert rigor by data-product value so critical marts get full SLO alerting and transient tables get a simple freshness ticket.
namingConventions: Name alerts by service, dimension, and condition, for example IngestionErrorBudgetBurnFast or RevenueMartFreshnessBreach.
Use consistent label keys across all rules: severity, team, pipeline, and service so routing and inhibition are predictable.
Name dedup keys stably from the failing object, for example airflow:<dag>:<task> or <pipeline>-<alertname>, never including the run id.
Name recording rules with a metric:aggregation:window pattern, for example job:ingestion_error_ratio:5m.
documentationStandards: Every paging alert links to a runbook with diagnosis queries, remediation steps, and escalation contacts.
Document each SLO's target, window, error budget, and the burn multipliers chosen for its alerts.
Maintain an on-call handbook covering severity definitions (P1-P4), page-vs-ticket-vs-log policy, and silencing procedures.
Record the rationale for each inhibition rule so future engineers understand the cause-effect assumption.
testingStrategies: Test routing and inhibition with `amtool config routes test` and unit tests before deploying config changes.
Fire synthetic alerts (fault injection: stop a producer, inject nulls) to verify the right severity pages and downstream alerts are inhibited.
Backtest burn-rate thresholds against historical incidents to confirm they would have paged for real outages and stayed quiet for tolerable blips.
Run periodic on-call fire drills and review the incident log so runbooks stay accurate and MTTA stays low.

commonMistakes.mistake: Paging on causes (host CPU, single task retry) instead of user-facing symptoms.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Cause metrics are easy to collect and it feels safer to alert on everything, so teams wire a page to every internal signal.
commonMistakes.impact: Dozens of non-actionable pages per shift bury the real incident, MTTA rises, and responders start ignoring the pager.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Alert on symptoms at the consumer boundary (freshness, success ratio, quality) and demote cause metrics to dashboards or tickets.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting one upstream failure spawn an alert storm of downstream alerts.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Each pipeline/table has its own independent alert and there is no expressed relationship between them.
commonMistakes.impact: A single Kafka outage generates 40 simultaneous pages, overwhelming the responder and hiding the actual root cause.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use grouping and inhibition so a critical upstream alert suppresses dependent downstream warnings, yielding one actionable page.

commonMistakes.mistake: Alerting immediately on any single error or low error rate.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Teams equate any error with a problem and set a threshold of 'greater than zero'.
commonMistakes.impact: Constant flapping pages for conditions well within the error budget, training everyone to dismiss the alerts.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use error-budget burn-rate alerts with a `for` duration and multi-window confirmation so only severe, sustained burns page.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shipping paging alerts with no runbook and no owner.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Alerts are added reactively during an incident and never revisited to add documentation or ownership.
commonMistakes.impact: Responders waste critical minutes re-diagnosing from scratch, MTTR grows, and orphaned alerts are eventually ignored.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Gate every new paging alert on a written, tested runbook, a severity, and an owning team label during code review.

comparisonSection.explanation: Symptom-based alerts fire on user-visible impact (data stale, wrong, or missing), so they are few and inherently actionable. Cause-based alerts fire on internal states (high CPU, a retried task) that the system often tolerates, producing volume and noise. Page on symptoms; keep causes on dashboards for diagnosis.

A single threshold either flaps (short window, false positives) or detects slowly (long window). Multi-window multi-burn-rate requires both a long and short window at each threshold, giving fast detection, high precision, and fast reset. It is more config but is the SRE-recommended default for SLOs.

Paging is for urgent, actionable, user-impacting conditions that need action within minutes. Tickets are for issues that can wait for business hours; logs are for record-only events. Defaulting everything to page manufactures fatigue, so classify each alert deliberately.

Inhibition and grouping express cause-effect and collapse a cascade into one page; deduplication maps repeats to one incident. Independent per-object alerts fire in parallel during a fan-out failure, burying the root cause. Suppression is essential once dependencies exist, with the caveat that it can hide a genuinely independent second failure.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is alert fatigue and why is it dangerous?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Alert fatigue is the desensitization that happens when on-call responders receive too many low-value, non-actionable, or duplicate alerts; they start ignoring the pager, so the one alert that actually matters gets missed. It is dangerous because it directly undermines reliability and burns out the team.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: A strong answer frames fatigue as a systems problem (bad alert design) rather than a people problem, and connects it to missed real incidents.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between a page, a ticket, and a log?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A page interrupts a human immediately for an urgent, actionable, user-impacting condition. A ticket queues an issue for business hours when action is needed but not urgently. A log is record-only for things that need no action. Every candidate alert should be deliberately classified into one of these.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want to hear that not everything should page and that the classification is based on urgency and actionability.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why is symptom-based alerting preferred over cause-based alerting?
intermediateQuestions.answer: There are many possible causes but few user-visible symptoms, so symptom alerts (data stale, wrong, or missing) are far fewer and inherently actionable, while cause alerts (high CPU, a retried task) fire for conditions the system often tolerates and create noise. Symptoms page; causes stay on dashboards to help diagnose once you are already looking.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: A good answer contrasts the cardinality of causes vs symptoms and ties it directly to reducing noise and fatigue.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does error-budget burn-rate alerting work?
intermediateQuestions.answer: An SLO implies an error budget of 1 minus the target. Burn rate is the observed error rate divided by that budget; a burn rate of 1 exhausts the budget exactly at the window's end. You page on fast burn (for example 14.4x, which exhausts a 30-day budget in about 2 days) and open tickets on slow burn (for example 6x), so you get fast detection of severe problems without paging on tolerable error rates.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: The interviewer checks that you can define burn rate as error_rate/(1-SLO) and explain why it reduces false pages compared to a fixed error threshold.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting and its trade-offs.
advancedQuestions.answer: It combines a long window (for precision, confirming the problem is sustained) and a short window (for fast reset, so the alert clears quickly once fixed) at each burn-rate threshold, and uses multiple thresholds (a high one that pages, a lower one that tickets). The trade-off is more configuration and needing multiple recording rules, but you get fast detection of severe outages, high precision (few false positives), and fast reset, which single-threshold alerts cannot achieve simultaneously.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Strong answers name both the long window (precision) and short window (reset) roles and the SRE Workbook default pairs (14.4x/6x).

advancedQuestions.question: How do you prevent alert storms when one upstream data source fails?
advancedQuestions.answer: Express the cause-effect relationship as suppression: group alerts by pipeline, deduplicate repeated events with a stable dedup key, and add an inhibition rule so a critical upstream alert (for example an ingestion burn) suppresses all downstream warnings sharing the same pipeline label. The result is one actionable page for the root cause instead of dozens of dependent pages. The caveat is that inhibition can hide a genuinely independent second failure, so scope it carefully with `equal` labels.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Mention grouping, dedup, and inhibition specifically, and acknowledge the risk that suppression can mask an independent failure.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your data on-call is getting 35 pages per shift, most are non-actionable, and MTTA has doubled. How do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: This is classic alert fatigue. First measure: pull the incident log and compute pages per shift, actionable percentage, and MTTA, and rank the noisiest alertnames. Then attack the top offenders: convert cause-based to symptom-based, downgrade non-urgent pages to tickets, add inhibition for cascades, and require runbooks for what remains.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Instrument the incident log and compute pages/shift, actionable %, and MTTA, then rank the top-10 noisiest alerts. Delete or downgrade always-firing and never-actioned rules, replace cause-based host alerts with SLO/freshness symptom alerts, add grouping and inhibition so upstream failures suppress downstream storms, and add a `for` duration plus multi-burn-rate confirmation to stop flapping. Attach runbooks and owners to every remaining paging alert, then review the fatigue metrics each handoff and keep pruning. Expect pages/shift to fall and actionable % and MTTA to recover as trust returns.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design an alerting system for a data platform with hundreds of pipelines feeding customer-facing dashboards, minimizing alert fatigue while guaranteeing critical incidents are caught.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Define SLOs (freshness and success ratio) at consumer boundaries, export SLIs to Prometheus, and use recording rules plus multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts. Route through Alertmanager with severity/team/pipeline labels: critical pages PagerDuty, warnings open tickets, info logs. Group by pipeline, deduplicate by stable key, and add inhibition so upstream failures suppress downstream storms. Attach runbooks and owners, add a heartbeat alert for the alerting path, and compute fatigue metrics from the incident log on a dashboard.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: SLO machinery and routing config cost engineering time and require good SLIs; aggressive inhibition risks masking an independent failure; slow burns intentionally do not page, which can surprise teams. Balance by tiering rigor by data-product value and scoping suppression with `equal` labels.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Anchor alert count to user-facing promises rather than component count: template alert rules across pipelines, use recording rules to keep evaluation cheap, keep routing trees shallow, avoid high-cardinality labels, and rely on grouping/inhibition so a fan-out failure still yields one page. Run Alertmanager clustered for HA.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Alerting design is engineering notifications so every page is urgent, actionable, and unique (symptom-based, SLO/error-budget-driven, deduplicated, grouped, and inhibited), which is the primary defense against alert fatigue.
keyConcepts: Alert on symptoms (user impact), not causes (internal metrics).
Drive paging from SLOs and error-budget burn rate.
Classify every alert as page, ticket, or log by urgency and actionability.
Collapse storms with grouping, deduplication, and inhibition.
Every paging alert needs a runbook and an owner.
Measure fatigue: pages per shift, actionable %, MTTA.
formulas: Time to exhaust budget = window / burn_rate
Fast-page threshold example: 14.4x for a 99.9% SLO over 30 days (~2 days to exhaust)
commands: Test Alertmanager routing: amtool config routes test --config.file=alertmanager.yml
List/expire silences: amtool silence query ; amtool silence expire <id>
Check firing alerts: amtool alert query
Validate Prometheus rules: promtool check rules rules.yml
PagerDuty trigger: POST https://events.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue with routing_key + dedup_key
interviewPoints: Symptom-based beats cause-based because symptoms are few and actionable.
Burn rate = error_rate / (1 - SLO); page fast burns, ticket slow burns.
Multi-window = long window for precision, short window for fast reset.
Inhibition + grouping + dedup collapse upstream storms into one page.
Fatigue is measurable (pages/shift, actionable %, MTTA) and must be tuned.
quickNotes: Not everything should page; default should be ticket or log.
Add a `for` duration to stop flapping alerts.
Use a stable dedup key (never the run id) so retries collapse.
Send resolve events so incidents auto-close and MTTR is accurate.
Run a heartbeat/dead-man's-switch so silent alerting is detected.
Review the top-10 noisiest alerts every on-call handoff.

keyTakeaways: Alert on user-visible symptoms (freshness, correctness, volume) rather than internal causes, because there are few symptoms and many causes, and symptom alerts are inherently actionable.
Drive paging from SLOs and error-budget burn rate, using multi-window multi-burn-rate rules so severe outages page fast while tolerable error rates become tickets.
Classify every alert as page, ticket, or log, and give every paging alert a runbook and an owner so responders always know the next step.
Collapse alert storms with grouping, deduplication, and inhibition so a single upstream failure produces one actionable page instead of dozens of downstream pages.
Alert fatigue is a measurable systems problem: track pages per shift, actionable percentage, and MTTA, and continuously prune the noisiest alerts to keep on-call sustainable and responsive.
